maintopic: EXPRESSION OF APPRECIATION FOR CANADIAN SYMPATHY FROM QUEEN JULIANA, THE NETHERLANDS
EXPRESSION OF APPRECIATION FOR CANADIAN SYMPATHY FROM QUEEN JULIANA, THE NETHERLANDS
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the house that I have received the following
communication from His Excellency the Ambassador of The Netherlands:
Dear Mr. Speaker:
Upon instructions received I have the honour to convey to you. on behalf of Her Majesty, Queen Juliana, the expression of Her Majesty's most sincere appreciation for the sympathy of the Canadian House of Commons to the people of The Netherlands who have been so severely stricken by the recent flood disaster.
The text of the resolution which was passed unanimously in the House of Commons on Monday, February 2, 1953, was transmitted to Her Majesty by the Canadian Ambassador at The Hague, and I now have the pleasure to convey to you Her Majesty's most heartfelt thanks.
Yours very sincerely,
A. h. j. LOVINK.

speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for giving me notice of his question. The matter to which he refers has been under consideration, but as yet no decision has been reached.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, January 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. McCann:
That a select committee be appointed on broadcasting to consider the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and to review the policies and aims of the corporation and its regulations, revenues, expenditures and development, with power to examine and inquire into the matters and things herein referred to and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and to send for persons, papers and records; that the committee have power to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be deemed advisable or necessary; that the committee have power to meet while the house is sitting; that the committee shall consist of the following members: Messrs, Beaudry, Boisvert, Breton, Carter, Courte-manche, Decore, Diefenbaker, Dinsdale, Fleming, Fulton, Gauthier (Portneuf), Gauthier (Sudbury), Hansell, Henry, Jones, Kirk (Digby-Yarmouth), Knight, MacLean (Queens), McCann, Murray (Cariboo), Mutch, Richard (Ottawa East). Riley,
Special Committee on Broadcasting Robinson, Smith (Moose Mountain), and Whitman; that standing orders 64 and 65 be suspended in relation thereto.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate, as Minister of Transport, because my department has some responsibility for the granting of licences for the operation of radio and television stations. Hon. members are aware that the procedure in this matter is that application is made to the Department of Transport for a licence to operate these stations. If the applications are found to be in order from the technical standpoint, or from other standpoints in so far as telecommunications are concerned, they are then referred to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for study and approval and for their recommendation as well. They then come back to the Minister of Transport, who has statutory authority to issue the licence.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with the principles upon which our television policy is based. But before doing so I should like to say something about the kind of nation that we are, about the kind of nation that we have succeeded in building because our principles, in a matter such as broadcasting and telecommunications, are all patterned upon the manner in which our country has been built. These are matters which, I submit with deference to the house, are of national concern. I should like, with your permission, to deal with them briefly.
There would be no Canadian nation at all if our founders had not realized that its creation, as well as its continued existence, required positive policies and careful planning in the fields of transport and communications, for instance, in the field of railways, in the field of national resources, in the field of banking and monetary problems as well as in many other fields. I am not thinking now, of course, of the kind of planning which our friends in the south corner of the house have reference to, but I am thinking of the co-ordinated efforts of public and private enterprise which have been characteristic of the growth of Canada from its earliest history.
The maintenance of our union, Mr. Speaker, was secured first, I suppose, by the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway which was constructed, established and completed by means of public as well as private enterprise. Our own Canadian banking system provided that we would have a national system of banking of our own. Then there came into being the Canadian National Railways, a system which by the assumption of several railway lines which
3008	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Broadcasting were not successful financially, ensured railway facilities which otherwise it would have been impossible to obtain.
Then again, because of that attitude of parliament in our country towards the Canadian National Railways, it was possible at public expense to assist private industry through the technical information that was obtained from the Canadian National Railways system. Again, more recently in our history, communications have been strengthened by the creation of publicly-owned national air lines and aid has been given continuously to private enterprise to operate air lines of their own. I could go on and deal with a number of other well-known examples of that sort. I have in mind at the moment Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation, which this parliament established as a crown company some years ago. Here we have it operating successfully in the field of telecommunications, of submarine cables and of Marconi wireless, side by side with private enterprise. Rates for carrying goods and persons have been set by a public body to ensure the best possible service to the public itself, and at the same time to ensure that the facilities themselves could remain in existence in order to bind our nation together.
These are just a few examples picked at random to show how the nation, through successive governments, has grown and developed as a result of conscious planning by the representatives of the people themselves. Why has this been done? It has been done, Mr. Speaker, because the people of this country have wanted to build a national home of their own and a nation whose destinies they control, notwithstanding the fact that we live in an interdependent world. What would have happened if Canadian governments had sat by and had not helped to build the Canadian Pacific Railway, for instance? What would have happened if they had let banks from other countries take charge of our financial affairs? If that had happened, would our people be as well off and as prosperous as they are today? I ask that question because our development and the growth of this nation have been the result of a partnership between private enterprise on the one hand and public enterprise on the other.
In every significant field or stage there have, of course, been struggles between those who put the national interest first and those who had regard primarily for their own personal profits. Fortunately, the national interest has usually won out. The interesting thing is that private enterprise has prospered and succeeded side by side. This


partnership has been successful although at times it has been acrimonious. But if we are to continue to grow and develop, that partnership must be maintained. That is the view of the Liberal party, Mr. Speaker, and we believe it is the only way in which we can have a truly Canadian nation. But the important thing is that today we have a strong and powerful nation, and one that is growing stronger day by day.
We could, I suppose, buy our jet engines in the United States, take out the props from under the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway and abandon Trans-Canada Air Lines, but where would Canada be if we were to do that? Much as we like our friends to the south and much as we want to get along with them, we would probably be the 49th state of the union if we were to act in that fashion.
How, I ask, does all this fit into the pattern of radio and television? The main requirement for a station is, of course, a frequency channel. Those frequencies or channels belong not to any individual group; they are part of the public domain, the property of the Canadian people. As such they should be developed for the use of all Canadians, not just for a small number of individuals, not just for those who are anxious to make a tremendous profit or who are anxious to make a killing at the hands of the public domain. Control over this matter should be designed to ensure that the freest possible expression of opinion should be maintained, not an expression of opinion such as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) or the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) would have us have by banning commentators with whom they do not agree or whom they do not like. There are, of course, as the house knows, differences of opinion as to who is like Mr. Eisenhower and who is not.
Here I should like to deal with a matter which my friend the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) referred to yesterday. He took to task the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) because he thought he had spoken in derogatory terms of a former prime minister of this country. I did not think that he had. However, that is not my point. My point is that today I wish to deal with a former prime minister, and to do so in very laudatory terms. I hope that my friend the hon. member for Greenwood and those who sit with him will be able not only to follow what I have to say in so far as he is concerned but will be able to follow through the policy which we are advocating at this

time, and which is based on the recommendations which were brought before parliament in those years. The late leader of the Conservative party, the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett, stated the principles on which he thought radio should operate in this country, and they are to be found in Hansard. The hon. member for Eglinton notwithstanding, the government believes that the same principles should continue to be applied in television today. In fact, because of the tremendous power and influence which this new medium is likely to have, we believe Mr. Bennett's dictum is more applicable today than it was then. I can do no better than to quote what Mr. Bennett said to this house on May 18, 1932, when he moved second reading of the bill respecting radio broadcasting. I ask those members on the opposition side particularly who have taken part in this debate and who have wandered away from the principles laid down by him to take note of what he said at that time, and I quote from page 3035 of Hansard:
First of all, this country must be assured of complete Canadian control of broadcasting from Canadian sources, free from foreign interference or influence. Without such control radio broadcasting can never become a great agency for the communication of matters of national concern and for the diffusion of national thought and ideals, and without such control it can never be the agency by which national consciousness may be fostered and sustained and national unity still further strengthened. Other and alternative systems may meet the requirements of other countries, and in any case it is not my purpose to comment unfavourably upon those systems. But it seems to me clear that in Canada the system we can most profitably employ is one which, in operation and control, responds most directly to the popular will and the national need. In this stage of our national development we have problems peculiar to ourselves and we must reach a solution of them through the employment of all available means. The radio has a place in the solution of all those problems. It becomes, then, the duty of parliament to safeguard it in such a way that its fullest benefits may be assured to the people as a whole.
And further on Lord Bennett continues:
No other scheme than that of public ownership can ensure to the people of this country, without regard to class or place, equal enjoyment of the benefits and pleasures of radio broadcasting.
And again:
The use of the air, or the air itself, whatever you may please to call it, that lies over the soil or land of Canada is a natural resource over which we have complete jurisdiction under the recent decision of the privy council.
In view of these circumstances and of the further fact that broadcasting is a science that is only yet in its infancy and about which we know little yet, I cannot think that any government would be warranted in leaving the air to private exploitation and not reserving it for development for the use of the people.
My hon. friend laughed as I began the recital of this statement a moment ago.
68108-191J
Special Committee on Broadcasting Well, he has a perfect right to do that, but I say those were the words of Mr. Bennett, those were the views which he expressed in 1932 on how radio should be operated in Canada; and to his eternal credit he never wavered, nor did he waver during the time that he was in the house, from those conclusions. We in the government think that the late Lord Bennett's views are still appropriate for today's conditions, and apply with even greater force in the field of television than they did in the field of broadcasting. Granted that the airwaves, through which television broadcasting takes place, belong to the public, it still is asked by many people:	Why, in a country where
private enterprise is encouraged and supported by the majority of the population, should there be public development and the public control of television broadcasting? Obviously there has to be some measure of public control, some policing of the air, or the right to broadcast would be worthless, because one station would be in interference with another, one frequency would overlap the other. As the house well knows, it is impossible to give two stations the same frequency. Obviously it follows that any Canadian with the necessary capital cannot just start to broadcast. He must first be allotted a frequency or an exclusive channel, whether it is in the field of broadcasting or in the field of television.
In other words, every private station which is allowed to broadcast is being given a special privilege which is not open to anyone else, and since it is a privilege to exploit the public domain and to try to make money out of the public domain, parliament has not only a perfect right, but it has a duty, to see to it that there is control over that kind of broadcasting, whether it be in one field or the other.
Now, then, what is the public interest? I am prepared to admit that if Canada were an island such as Australia the same dangers would not obtain for our country as it would for other countries, because Australia is thousands of miles away from other countries. We in Canada have to live beside a much more populous and wealthier country which extends along the whole of our southern border. If we are to maintain our Canadian traditions and our Canadian policy, as we have maintained them in the field of radio, then we must see to it that there is a strict control in so far as these stations are concerned.
A generation ago patriotic Canadians like the late Lord Bennett and the late Mr. Dafoe were seriously concerned lest radio broadcasting should fall entirely under the

Special Committee on Broadcasting control of American chains. This was not because we did not like the people of the United States. It was not because we did not want to listen to a good many of the American programs. It was simply because we wanted some of our broadcasting, as much as we could reasonably afford, to be of Canadian content and of Canadian origin, and I think most of us wanted it to be distinctly Canadian, even if it developed a little more slowly and might not be technically as good at the start as that produced in the United States.
Well, I am not going to make any comparisons between broadcasting in our country and broadcasting in the United States; but I do think that the existence of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has contributed to keeping this country definitely and distinctively Canadian. Had it not been for the C.B.C. we would have had a condition in this country such as that which the Winnipeg Free Press feared as far back as 1932 when it wrote editorials on the subject. I have one in my hand dated Wednesday, April 13, 1932, which pointed to the strength of the monopolies in the field of radio in the United States and expressed the fear that those companies should move into Canada and take over our radio. Just let me quote that portion of the editorial:
The radio issue now being decided at Ottawa is quite simple and very easily grasped. There is a choice between a national system and the handing over of the radio-supporting public of Canada to the radio monopolies of the United States. All the pleas put forth on behalf of private control of radio in Canada, no matter how plausibly presented nor how strongly backed by eminent figures in the world of finance, are in support of a system which in its practical working out will make Canada a subordinate annex of United States radio-land and give the final (if concealed) voice in the decision of how radio is to be operated in Canada to purely commercial interests, American in character. The day of the small detached and supposedly independent radio station is about over in Canada. If the field is left to private enterprise, there will be rapid consolidation of these stations into a combination. We shall have a privately-owned monopoly of the air, and this monopoly will operate in harmony with the great radio monopoly of the United States-the harmony that always exists between the boss that gives orders and the dependent subordinate who obeys them.
If that was true in 1932 with reference to radio, a fortiori it is still true today wtih reference to television. Let me go on and say this:	What I believe the people of
Canada want more than anything else is that in the field of television the programs should be of Canadian origination and of Canadian content and should not be canned programs coming in from the United States. Most people have formed the impression that television can have a much more powerful
[Mr. Chevrier.l

influence on the minds of people than radio. In fact it can have a tremendous influence on the minds of our children, and for that reason it is all the more necessary for us to see to it that a policy is worked out which will protect those interests.
I think that in the field of television there is a graver danger to our distinctive Cana-dianism from American control than there would have been from American control of sound broadcasting.
In other words the essential reason for public development of television in this country is that we want a reasonable proportion of what we look at and, more particularly, what our children look at, both popular programs and cultural programs, to be produced in Canada by Canadians, about Canada. That does not mean-
And that is what your television policy will defeat, the way you are going about it now.

My hon. friend says that that is what our television policy will defeat. That is just what the policy he is advocating will accomplish; and if he will allow me to continue my remarks he will see from them that the policy advocated by him and by his leader, and those of his party who have spoken in this debate, is just the kind of policy which will allow the television operators from the United States to move in and take over the field. Of that there can be no doubt.
You are hopelessly wrong.

We shall see about that.
I was going on to say, in my statement with reference to American influence on television, that I do not want to be misconstrued by having it said that we do not want broadcasting outlets or programs which would emanate from the United States. On the contrary we hope that there will be programs from the United States. We want programs from the United States. Some of them we like; many of them we do not like. But we do not want, above all, that these programs will come over and be in a position to monopolize the field.
That does not mean that our broadcasting outlets will not select a good many American programs-and perhaps a good many American programs of which the hon. member for Eglinton or even the Leader of the Opposition will not approve. But, after all, we cannot all have the same judgment as to what is or what is not a good program. No one is silly enough to suggest that all television broadcasts should be Canadian; and that is not what I am advocating. But we do want a

substantial part of that to be Canadian. And it is essential that they should be, if this country is to remain Canada.
Now then, dealing more particularly with the interruption of my hon. friend: It is perfect nonsense-and I hope the Leader of the Opposition will excuse me if I take that word from his vocabulary, because he seems to be fond of using it-it is perfect nonsense for anyone to suggest that private enterprise in Canada, left to itself, will provide Canadian programs. People who invest their money in private television stations, like people who invest their money in other business enterprises, are investing that money to make money. And I am not criticizing them for that. They will certainly invest their money where they will make the profit-by importing American programs-if on the other hand they will make very little or no profit by originating Canadian programs.
Obviously there is far more money to be made-in some cases 50 per cent, 100 per cent, 200 per cent or 500 per cent-from these canned programs that would come in from the United States, far more than would be made otherwise by producing and originating Canadian programs.
So, for that reason, it is my humble view that private broadcasters should not be allowed the full field, as suggested by my hon. friend. Indeed, the only way in which we will get Canadian programs is by-
May I ask the minister a question?
Make your own speech later.
Who is the hon. member to whom the minister is referring, and to whom he attributes the assertion that all broadcasting should be private?

I was referring to the interruption made by my hon. friend earlier to which he wanted a reply, and I gave it to him. And, if he will just hold himself, he will see, later on in my remarks, whom I am referring to. But I repeat-
On a question of privilege; I infer from the minister's response to my question that he seems to be referring to me.
If the cap fits, wear it.
I wish to make it clear that I have not said any such thing at any time. Certainly it does not bear any resemblance to anything I have ever said.

You have been converted. You are the first convert.
Special Committee on Broadcasting
My hon. friend should not be so nervous about what he has said or what he has not said. But I would like to continue my remarks.
Then speak the truth.

Oh, we will see, I hope, before I take my seat, just who is telling the truth. The only way, in my humble opinion, in which we will get Canadian programs is by some form of public provision for their production, and some form of public requirement for their dissemination.
That, very simply, is the reason why parliament decided, in Mr. Bennett's day, and has never seen fit to alter the decision, that the national agency-now the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-should have the primacy in the field of broadcasting.
Why then, it may be asked, have any private stations at all? Why not give the whole field to the C.B.C.? There are some who advocate that course; but that is not the position taken by the government. Our view is that the private station, also, has a place in the broadcasting field, not as a competitor of the C.B.C. but as a complement to the C.B.C.
If the C.B.C. had the field all to itself in sound broadcasting or in television, there would be a real danger of uniformity and of complacency. There would not be the same incentive to provide local programs to meet local desires. Moreover, it is still early to say just how many television stations can really be operated profitably.
How many are, in fact, really needed to provide decent public service? That is another question to which consideration should be given. There is an element of risk-taking, an element of enterprise, in the establishment of stations in medium and smaller centres. And this is an appropriate field for local initiative, for private enterprise, and for all the extra incentives and ingenuity likely to be called forth by the necessity to make an enterprise pay.
That is why the government feels, at this stage, that we should have in television, as in sound broadcasting, a combination of public and private stations. But there is one difference between the two. For the present, at least, we are proposing to grant only one licence in each centre.
Why this policy? Well, there are several reasons for it. One of the most important is that we feel that there is only a limited amount of capital available in Canada for investment in television stations, and, since television stations can be established only by use of the public domain, that they should be situated so as to provide service to the largest possible number of Canadians, from

Special Committee on Broadcasting one station, before anyone is allowed to provide the people in any community with two stations.
I am sure that, except for a few individuals and corporations directly interested, this policy will appeal to the vast majority of Canadians as a reasonable and fair one. I know that there are certain interests which would like to provide stations in the more populous centres which have been reserved for the time being exclusively to C.B.C. It may well be that in time the policy will have to be amended; it may well be that plans can be worked out which will be fair to the public for the establishment of private stations in those centres. But in the early stages, if we are to have the production of Canadian material broadcast by television, the C.B.C. must have access to the areas where large revenues can be earned to finance Canadian production for national distribution both by the C.B.C. and by the private stations. That is what can be called the basic economics of the television policy. That is the television policy of the government.
To sum it up, it is the traditional policy of the Liberal party to protect the public domain for the benefit of the Canadian people and in the field of broadcasting and television, through public development and public control, to make sure there is a sufficient Canadian content in the broadcasting to keep Canada Canadian. At the same time it is our policy through the granting of licences to private stations, but not to chains of private stations, to provide scope for local development and for genuine enterprise and risk-taking in the development of this new medium of mass communication and mass entertainment.
One other thing. We do not think that the taxpayers as a whole should be required to finance the public development of television. We think it should be financed as far as possible by the television users, either through advertising revenue earned by both public and private stations or through the special excise on radio and television parts as stated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his budget speech. This is a tax which is to be paid only by the users and which in future is to be devoted to the maintenance and development of our Canadian system.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that I was unable to be here on January 27 when this debate was begun, but I am very happy that I am here today and able to take part in a discussion of radio and television broadcasting, in which for many years I have been interested. I regret that this year I am not on the radio committee again, but one of our representatives on the committee, in the person of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), placed our views before this house very ably and well when he spoke on the first occasion that this resolution was before the house.
When the last committee reported to this house it reiterated the statements of previous committees all through the years as I have understood them. You will recollect, sir, that in December-I think December 14, 1951- the last report on radio broadcasting was tabled in this chamber. The committee said this:
Your committee shares the view of the royal commission-
That is the commission we usually refer to as the Massey commission.
-and of previous committees of the house that the national broadcasting service carried on by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is essential in the development of our national life in Canada and is efficiently performing an extremely valuable and important function.
There may be some disagreement with the last clause, but I do not think there should be any disagreement with the statement that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is essential in the development of our national life in this country. The committee had this
'Mr. Fournier (Maisonneuve-Rosemont).]

to say on the topic which now forms the major part of the discussion on television:
Your committee is strongly impressed with the vital need for the development of a television system that is essentially Canadian and which gives expression in this new form of broadcasting to Canadian ideas and aspirations. It agrees with the royal commission that the situation must be avoided under which commercial pressures will lead to the major part of the material on Canadian channels being non-Canadian.
I think both these recommendations to the house were sound and indeed were worth reiterating on that occasion, as the committee had reiterated them on many previous occasions.
At this time Canadians are being subject to ever-increasing propaganda from the United States-and when I refer to the United States I want it clearly understood that I am not unfriendly to the United States; but I am anxious that this country, Canada, shall remain an independent entity on the North American continent. I recollect well that it was Sir John A. Macdonald who said, and the Right Hon. R. L. Borden who reiterated: "A British subject I was born, a British subject I will die". Well, I can say, of course, a British subject I was born, as most hon. members in this house can, and as a Canadian citizen I hope to die. I believe that we have to do everything we can to preserve our national identity. As a matter of fact we are subject, as I have said, to ever-increasing propaganda from our great neighbour to the south. Our cheap magazines and literature, so largely read by our young people, originate mostly on the other side of the line, and more and more economically the basic resources of this country are being exploited by United States' corporations and their Canadian subsidiaries. And altogether it behooves this parliament to take every conceivable step within our power to maintain the national integrity of this country and to maintain our national independence. Indeed, I believe that the national independence of this country has already been jeopardized economically and culturally by operations of corporations and of organizations originating in the United States.
Television is probably the most potent force for propaganda or for education that is now, or ever has been, available to man. Its misuse by those who wish to use it as a commercial organ dependent largely, as they must be if they are going to run continuous programs, on United States material, could destroy the whole fabric of our independent national existence.
Propaganda of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters for the private control of television, whether they realize it or not,

and of those who associate themselves with that propaganda, is in effect, in my opinion, treasonable to this country. Those who consciously or unconsciously echo their demand for the private control of television and broadcasting are, in my opinion, encouraging propaganda which eventually will destroy the identity and the independence of this Canadian nation. And if we allow a new and more powerful way of American influence to enter into Canadian homes, whether it be under the sacred name of private enterprise or not, we shall prevent the development of a distinctive Canadian society of any permanence.
As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) indicated this afternoon in some of the examples he gave, this parliament ever since confederation has been called upon to make decisions, decisions which were designed to establish and maintain Canada as an independent, distinct North American nation. In 1867 those scattered provinces of North America were bound together under the British North America Act in confederation. Shortly afterwards, in order to bind this country more closely, as the Minister of Transport indicated this afternoon, a railway was built across Canada with large grants of public lands and money to secure what the union already visualized and to establish the nation, as the main entrance to this building indicates, stretching from sea to sea.
May I point out to my hon. friends of the Conservative party that that indeed was the principal objective of the national policy of Sir John A. Macdonald in 1878. Whether we agree with that tariff policy or not, that was the objective Sir John A. Macdonald had in view at that time. Indeed it had been the motive of his life and policies before that time. I hope that my hon. friends and others in this house have read that very interesting, unusual and exceedingly well-written biography of "John A. Macdonald, the Young Politician" by Professor Donald Creighton. I regard that as one of the most significant and best pieces of literature produced at any time in Canada for Canadians, and by a Canadian. I think it is something we should all read and recommend.
The national policy of 1878 was designed to that end, and in 1919 it was Sir Robert Borden who placed Canada's signature on the treaty of Versailles, in Canada's own right-as Canada. This represented another step in the promotion of our national development as an independent nation.
I am not going into the setting up of the Canadian National Railways, and other aspects of this problem. But since 1930 parliament has made many decisions designed
Special Committee on Broadcasting to protect and to develop Canadian institutions and Canadian citizenship. And no man was more anxious to do that than the late Lord Bennett. I am not going to quote, as I have often done, from his many speeches in the house-some of which I had the privilege of hearing-regarding Canadian broadcasting. But Mr. Bennett's speeches at all times indicate clearly the importance of radio broadcasting as a means of promoting Canadian unity and Canadian consciousness.
He stated clearly again and again that, because of its importance, radio broadcasting could not be left to private commercial interests either to develop or to control in any particular. Indeed, it was Mr. Bennett who wanted a limitation placed upon the power private radio stations would obtain under the licence from the Department of Transport. And I regret to say that, step by step, over the years, the original conception of the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act has been largely discounted-I shall not say, "set aside"-by parliament, when private radio stations have been allowed to go in power from 1,000 to 5,000, 10,000 or even 50,000 kilowatts. That was something never intended when that act was passed by parliament.
In the main, in spite of what I have just said, the successors to Mr. Bennett, the Liberal government-and perhaps under its new leadership it might be considered to be a somewhat different government-but at any rate the successors to Mr. Bennett have tried invariably, I think, to do the same thing with regard to broadcasting. And it was with these ends in view, as the Minister of Transport said this afternoon, that parliament established a national banking system, set up the Bank of Canada, to supervise and control our Canadian banks and financial corporations under public control and, so far as possible, in the public interest. Whether it succeeded in doing that is another question not to be debated this afternoon.
Then, the Canadian Citizenship Act was passed for the same purpose. And lastly, and perhaps most important of all-because, as it were, it is a culmination in the cultural field of national policy-we set up a royal commission known as the Massey commission. And we set up that Massey commission to see how Canada's cultural development could be maintained, how it could be promoted. We have now before us the recommendations and report of that commission.
And so I would say this, that if at this juncture we allow the newest and most important educational or, if you wish so to describe it, propaganda instrument, to pass out of complete control of the public, through

Special Committee on Broadcasting parliament, we shall undermine the decisions which for the last 86 years have been the basic steps in developing Canada as a conscious, separate and independent nation.
To my mind those who would set the clock back at this stage, and hand over this most potent force to private interests, which of necessity would rely largely upon programs originating in the United States, are in effect, while they may not realize it-and I am not accusing them of it consciously-subversive of our national interests. And indeed when we hear so much about the freedom connected with radio broadcasting, we must conclude that their activities and proposals are subversive of the freedom of this country as an independent and distinct nation.
I want it to be clearly understood that in expressing these views I am not, nor is the C.C.F. movement, narrowly nationalistic. We believe that each national culture should be promoted, because eventually it will contribute to a world society in which individual cultures and abilities will be integrated but will not be smothered. That, indeed, is the concept of Canada as a confederation of two great peoples with different cultures, joined together, integrated and making a joint contribution, but neither one smothering the other.
Indeed, I would go beyond that and say that within our national boundaries we have representatives of other nations and other cultures-Ukrainian, Polish, Italian, Norwegian, Swedish and many others. All these should be encouraged to maintain their peculiar national cultures, but also become integrated into a Canadian society, a Canadian nation.
And so I say that what I have been saying is not narrowly nationalistic. When I say this I wish merely to point out that I am endeavouring to place before the house the danger of allowing this great instrument of education or of propaganda to be used to subvert Canadian independence, Canadian ideals and Canadian culture-all of which could easily be done if we were to rely upon private television organizations importing, as they would have to, programs from the United States.
There is a difference between an unhealthy chauvinistic nationalism and a pride in a distinctive national culture and endeavour. And it is that pride of distinctive culture and national endeavour that leads me to say what I am saying this afternoon.
The clamour for private television stations is due largely to the natural desire of our people to enjoy television; and that is being capitalized upon by organizations that want
[Mr. Coldwell.l

to make money out of that natural desire for television. May I say that I share the desire to see some television in Canada. I know, perhaps as well as anyone in the house, the blessings that radio broadcasting has brought to people who are unable to leave their homes or their rooms. I know perfectly well that television will bring additional joy to that group of people, provided we get the decent and proper type of programs to show them.
And so I say I share that desire; and I think parliament should appropriate sufficient funds so that television under public ownership and public control can be effective, and so that stations to give television can be established to serve all parts of Canada. Our people have a right to a nation-wide service. I think, even if it requires large amounts of money to be appropriated by parliament, that every attempt should be made, for example, to establish stations in Regina, Saskatoon, Calgary and Edmonton, or those other parts of Canada which at the moment seem to be left out. I think we owe it to the people in those regions to establish these stations if we are to safeguard television for Canada and offset the propaganda of the C.A.B. throughout those regions. We should do everything we can to establish stations at as early a date as possible. There is no reason why we in Ottawa or the people in Toronto and Montreal should enjoy this service, largely at public expense. I do not for one moment believe, except in the initial stage, that the excise tax on television sets and radios will entirely compensate the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the services which they will be called upon to render. So I should like to see all our centres in Canada served so that there will be complete coverage of the whole country even if this involves further financial aid to the C.B.C.
Our people have a right to a nation-wide service. This service should be national in the best sense of the word and certainly should not be left to advertisers, to profit-seekers, yes, to hucksters whose only incentive is that of profit and gain. The incentive for television, and indeed for radio, should be service to Canada as a nation and to its people as citizens. To adopt any other policy would in my opinion be an act of treachery and treason on the part of this parliament to those who for the last 86 years have endeavoured to make Canada a free, independent and distinct nation. At page 303 of the report of the Massey commission we find these words:
That no private television broadcasting stations be licensed until the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has available national television programs

and that all private stations be required to serve as outlets for national programs.
After going across the country and hearing representations from all sorts of people the Massey commission made a recommendation which I think was a sound one. 1 am not saying that under such a system there would not be room, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has stated, for some private television stations, but they should be under distinct control and should be required to take from the C.B.C. such television programs as originate in the C.B.C. studios in this country.
I do not want to see repeated what has happened largely with our radio. I do not want to see an organization like the Canadian Association of Broadcasters being able to place itself in the position of saying that they are equal to or competitive with the national broadcasting system. I want to emphasize what the Minister of Transport said, and what others no doubt have said and will say, that the granting of an air channel or a television channel-there are fewer of those-is the granting of a monopoly to a private corporation if it is granted to a corporation. No one else can use that channel. There is no freedom of expression as a right on that channel.
We see now that the C.A.B. want to go one step forward and place themselves in the position of being able largely to control public thinking by demanding the right to editorialize on the air through the private stations. I think that that is something that should be prevented at all costs. The C.A.B. has built itself up until today it is a powerful propaganda agency operating as I believe against the best interests of the country, and from my point of view likely to destroy the independence of this country and place us more and more under the cultural and economic control of the United States. As I have said already, I regard that as a treasonable and subversive activity, just as treasonable and subversive as the activities of those who would sell our country to a communist power or to Russia. I can see little difference between the two.
We welcome, because the people of Canada welcome, the abolition of the licence fee. I know that there were many people who could not pay the fee and that there were others who did not pay the fee, and therefore perhaps it was an unfair levy. But I know of no payment that an individual could make which brought more value into his home than the $2.50 he paid to the C.B.C. as a licence fee to operate his radio. However, some people did not pay it and others could not pay it so we decided to abolish it. But I do want to say that in my opinion there was nothing for which we obtained such great
Special Committee on Broadcasting value as we obtained for this $2.50 licence fee. I think of the many hours of delight that I have had in listening to opera, to symphonies, to drama, to forums of information-
To hockey games.

Yes, to hockey games. Many people enjoy the hockey games. The variety provided by the C.B.C. is something to be commended. Of course there are some programs which I could criticize most adversely, but then there are other advertising programs I can acclaim as being good programs. I think the program sponsored by Canadian Industries Limited called "Singing Stars of Tomorrow" is one of the most worth-while radio programs we have. One is glad indeed that there are some good advertising programs. This one is a jewel amid a great deal of muck and drivel that goes for advertising over radio stations.
I want to see preserved the national interest. I believe that Canada's ultimate independence is linked with education. These are the two most powerful instruments of education that we have today-radio and television. Let us keep them Canadian. Let us not allow ourselves to be sold down the river even to a great and friendly neighbour to the south.
I want to conclude my remarks with this thought. Today once again, as in 1867, in 1878, in 1919, in 1932 and all down the years, this parliament is called upon once again to make a decision involving the future of our country. Let that decision be that we are going to keep this great educational facility for the development of Canadian citizenship and the preservation of Canada as an independent North American nation with its own distinctive culture.

Mr. Speaker, it was nice to see the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Caldwell) back in the house again in good form this afternoon. In the main I share his views and I hope they will prevail. 1 agree that all our thinking on television must start with one basic principle. I cannot put it better than it was put by the minister in charge of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation who said:
Television is probably the most effective method yet devised by man for making an impression on the minds of people.
The importance of television is being appreciated more and more from day to day. Its social implications, its potential for moulding the thinking habits of Canadians, cannot be exaggerated. Sight has been joined to sound and will be the medium of influence in the privacy of our homes. Like radio, it will open

Special Committee on Broadcasting up a new world for great segments of the population. The world of education, amusement, sports, entertainment, culture and events will be brought into our homes. The young will find it useful in their schools and in the universities.
I bring to the attention of the house that here is an opportunity to pioneer, to lead the world, in using television as an instrument of education. Our universities, our colleges and our public schools are bubbling with talent. If we give them opportunities to produce programs they may not click the first time, but they will in time. There is a place for television in the classrooms as well as in the homes, for the education of the young as well as the adult.
It follows that television has tremendous possibilities for good and for something very much worse. Properly developed it can become an unparalleled instrument for education and for cultural and social development-everything that radio, with a few notable exceptions, was not. Improperly handled television can follow the worst in radio, with banal entertainment, the inevitable and nauseating commercials, a combination of intellectual trash and social unconcern.
Today television in Canada is at the crossroads. We have to decide which course it shall take. We have the opportunity, as no other country has at the present time, to usher in a new tomorrow for television. Our only guide to the future is the history of radio broadcasting, although obviously the development of television will be much faster and it will be a greater and more significant force for good or for ill.
We now have in Canada 250,000 television sets. Forty per cent of them are in the Toronto-Hamilton area; 21-5 per cent are in the Windsor area; 18 per cent of them are in the Montreal area; and 14 per cent are in the Niagara area. Within the next four years we will have a million sets in Canada.
I speak as a believer in the public ownership and the public control of licence. The public television channels should be used only in the public interest. I am a firm believer in the value of the C.B.C. It has for many years given us a standard of excellence in culture, entertainment, events and information which is unique in North America. I hail the government's decision to place television in the same competent hands and to administer its use in the same impartial manner.
I believe the Canadian people are well satisfied with the status of broadcasting in this country. They will be equally satisfied if we can develop a television system designed to reach and serve the greatest


possible number of Canadians and link together all parts of Canada. Television must remain the property of the people and must be developed and controlled by the people-
Hear, hear.

-and not by the promoters of beer, cosmetics and patent medicines. Television must belong neither to the "long-hairs" nor to the "crew-cuts". I am opposed to excessive artiness as I am opposed to the pitchman's taste.
To understand the problem it is essential to have some background, in order that we may not make the same mistake twice in one generation. There are three possible courses open for the development of television. We can leave it to private interests. We tried that in radio and it did not work because private radio stations became outlets for United States chains; and so we created the C.B.C. We may develop it under a mutual system of public ownership and publicly controlled private enterprise; that is the government's proposal. The third course is that we may keep it strictly under public control; I am afraid it is a little too late for that now.
So far as private development of television is concerned, I can only say: Look at the state of commercial radio and television in the United States. Further comment, to me, seems superfluous. Still, we must deal with the arguments propounded by those who advocate privately-owned television. They say it was private enterprise that developed radio in Canada in the 1920's. It is true that private interests began radio broadcasting in Canada; but its supporters neglect to mention that they failed to meet Canadian needs, to serve outlying districts or to develop any distinctive form of Canadian radio. They were merely outlets for United States programs, and so it became necessary to create the C.B.C.
I disagree with those who believe we should pattern our television system on that of the United States. I rebel against the unending and constant exhortations to buy beer, cigarettes, detergents, dill pickles, and lazy laxatives with or without chlorophyll. I am opposed to having my viewing restricted to those programs which advertisers feel will sell those products. American television is not all bad. Nothing is. Some of it is good, and some of it is very good; but it is submerged in a flood of bad programs. Believe me, if the Americans had it to do all over again they certainly would correct their overemphasis on advertising. If they had our opportunity, United States television would be different, yes, very much different.

The more important feature is that the possibilities latent in television-and we have only to guess at some of them-are tremendous. We cannot afford to have television get out of public hands. Someone must always have the responsibility of answering for it on the floor of this house of parliament. As an example of joint public and private ownership we have the C.B.C. with an excellent record of service and a high calibre of programs. There must be room in our television schedules for those types of programs which are not commercially popular but which provide interesting viewing for Canadians. There must be a place in Canadian television for educational programs. If we do not apply common sense now in establishing the Canadian television system we will find the most powerful means of communication yet devised by man degenerating into a living room billboard.
The commercial interests in this country are very impatient. They want one of our greatest natural resources, our invaluable television channels which are limited in number, thrown open to anyone who has money enough to open a station, thus granting to a handful of people the right to give us only the programs which they want to broadcast, and which will sell their products. What they want is an advertising heaven on earth.
I do not object to advertising. As a matter of principle, I welcome it. I enjoy it, and it can be useful and intelligent. It must not, however, monopolize our television channels with a steady parade of comedy, quizzes, panel programs, western movies-bad ones at that-and gangster films which are the daily diet of the United States television viewers. We must escape from those who think television is God's gift to advertising. I admit that television is the greatest medium of advertising known to mankind, and private television is doing its best to hit the jackpot with it.
There is not much need for me to deal with the third point, which is that of public control; but it is worth noting that as an example of public control we have Great Britain, where both radio and television are state enterprises. The cultural level of the B.B.C., with its three great program divisions, is unquestionably the highest in the world. As for British television, all observers are in agreement that it is artistically and technically far ahead of its closest competitor in the United States.
We know that television is very costly. A single unit, with all the necessary equipment, is estimated to cost in the neighbourhood of
Special Committee on Broadcasting $1 million. We know the short range of its transmission, some 40 or 50 miles, which makes necessary a network of relay towers across this country. There are few people in this country who singly or even collectively have a million dollars. We cannot afford to put this tremendous medium of communication, with all its potential, into the hands of a few wealthy people. They own too many radio stations now. Concentration of this important medium of communication may well be a danger and a hazard to our liberty.
I read from the Globe and Mail of March 14, J. V. McAree's column, in which he says:
Roy Thomson, having bought the Advertiser and two other suburban papers from the Charters Publishing Company, now owns fifteen or sixteen newspapers from Quebec to Vancouver and one in Florida. He also owns half a dozen radio stations.
I have nothing against Mr. Thomson. He is a very fine gentleman. I merely read the extract in order to make a point which I think is important. In years past we have been concerned about one-newspaper towns, and in later years about chain newspapers. In more recent times, newspapers and radio stations in the same city have all too frequently been owned by the same people. Today we face a new problem; I ask this house and the country, is it in the public interest that the newspaper, radio and television stations in a city should be owned and controlled by the same people? I ask another question. Is it in the public interest that the radio and television stations of a city should be owned and controlled by the same people? Are we not being party to the building up of a colossal mass-communications empire, a combine which we shall some day have to break up? Why permit the building of that empire at the present time?
We know that Canada, with its sparse population and great land area, presents a very difficult and expensive proposition for television. The result must inevitably be that commercial television will be concentrated in the Montreal and Toronto areas which comprise the best two commercially profitable fields for exploitation. That is the very thing we cannot allow. Television in Canada must be television for all the people, and not for just a few of the people. The opponents of the government's television policy are going about the country saying that Toronto and Montreal are the chosen people in so far as television is concerned. Nothing is further from the truth. Toronto and Montreal have television stations because they reach 30 per cent Gf the total population of Canada, and because they are the great sources of revenue. It is true that St. James

street and Bay street have money, and television is put there for the purpose of digging some of it out for the benefit of the rest of the people of Canada. The revenue derived from these two cities will make it possible to have television in the smaller centres much sooner and much cheaper.
The private stations are only interested in the populous centres, and would leave the rest of the country literally in the dark.
What else is the C.B.C. doing?

Private interests want the easy pickings. The C.B.C. will get around to the rest of the country. Now that the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has interjected, I must read him the statement of his leader in order that I may emphasize what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has already placed upon the record. I quote from the Globe and Mail of December 9, 1952, which states:
The Progressive Conservative chieftain held that Canadian television development should be the other way around. Private interests should be free to invade those areas most suitable to them while the C.B.C. should undertake to put television into areas where the ordinary financial returns will not justify private investment.
I re-emphasize what the minister has today placed upon the record. There is more to it than merely that. The C.B.C. production centres must be located where the greatest amount of talent is available, where there are musicians, actors, writers and those with related talents required by television. Undoubtedly there is very good talent to be found in Moncton, Prince Albert, Trail, and other centres; yet it is not available in sufficient numbers to supply a television service operating on a national basis. It is my hope that those in charge of Canadian television will recognize that our primary responsibility will be in the development and presentation of Canadian talent. They must open new doors to our people of creative talent in order to give them opportunities for expressions which hitherto they have not had in this country, and have had to seek in the United States and Great Britain. We must submerge our inferiority complex with regard to native talent and give it a chance.
I cannot resist the temptation, and the house will forgive me, to take a well deserved smack at my own city of Toronto, particularly at the Canadian National Exhibition. When I speak of giving our own talent an opportunity, I think a good start would be for our Canadian talent to have the opportunity of carrying the entertainment portion of the Canadian National Exhibition at Toronto. I think an all-Canadian show would break all box office records. What is more, it would 
break down the inferiority complex for which there is no reason or excuse. Canadian entertainment has never been given a fair chance to carry this show. It has always been written off without a chance to measure up. The time has come for a new approach.
We have spent substantial sums of money in the investigation of United States, European and British television. We know something of the mistakes made by others, and we should avoid the same pitfalls. We must profit from their experience but we must not be hurried, in spite of what anyone says about not providing television to the whole of Canada overnight. There may be advantages in not being too hurried. It is often said that colour television is just around the corner, and we may avoid putting our people to double expense.
It is quite obvious from what has been said on behalf of private enterprise that they want to get on the gravy train. But commercial television could not possibly provide us with the service which we have a right to expect across Canada. The only alternative is for a balanced service which only C.B.C. can give. As we have done with other great enterprises, because of our relatively small population scattered over great distances, we must continue to do those things collectively which we cannot do individually. Thus I share with the government the view that our needs can best be met by public ownership with reasonable financial support, supplemented by publicly controlled private enterprise.
I recognize that private radio stations have been turning licence into privilege and now claim with some force and recognition a vested interest. Nonetheless, we must continue to lay stress on the need to keep use of the airways free from vested private interests.
The government have said that they will build television stations in Vancouver, Winnipeg and Halifax in addition to those in Toronto and Montreal, and that applications from private stations will be considered for other points not within the coverage of C.B.C. stations. There will be ample opportunity for private enterprise in television.
The recommendation by Sir John Aird, the father of publicly-owned broadcasting, whose emphasis was on "freedom of the air", was reiterated and supported by Right Hon. R. B. Bennett who declared that "the airways belong to the people". The Massey commission also recommended a system of public ownership. I am firmly convinced that each was right in his time.
When we support the C.B.C., we are providing favourable conditions for a service from which everyone will benefit eventually.

We must ask ourselves the question whether we will control television or whether it will control us; whether it will be controlled by the profit-seekers and advertisers or whether it will remain under control of the people. These are the formative years and we must make up our minds. As citizens and listeners we must ask ourselves the question: Are we going to have something to say about the kind of programs that are going to be levelled at us, or are we prepared to turn the matter over and put it into the hands of others who are not answerable to the people? I have a word to say to C.B.C. television. If through lack of competition they become complacent or self-satisfied or heavy from sitting on-they know what I mean-we shall have to re-examine our policy. They carry a very heavy responsibility. I have already indicated what we do not want in television. It is much more difficult to explain what we do want. We may not all agree. This much I can say with certainty. We want something that is typically, exclusively and distinctly Canadian. I cannot describe it, but I am thinking of wheat fields, a sunset on the prairies, rural Quebec, pea soup, maple sugar, a hockey broadcast on Saturday night, Cathedral Grove, bluenoses, the Grey Cup game, spiritual and moral values, social justice such as the universal old age pension, freedom, peace, immigrants, space and growth, vitality and wide horizons. And I am thinking of people, yes, people as fine as any that have come down the pike of time, who want to be Canadians, just Canadians, destined to contribute something of value to our generation and to history.
