Mr. Speaker, on Friday when the house rose I had made a few remarks on this bill, and I should now like to add a few more. I told 
the minister that we welcomed his enunciation of policy on the question of natural gas, and I reminded him that what he had said was an echo of what had been said more than once on this side of the house.
This is a matter of great importance and is almost certain to become of increasing importance; therefore I think it is worth spending a few minutes to put the record quite straight. I therefore propose to put on record a few of the statements which have been made. I welcome the minister's statement. It is almost like the return of the prodigal son to hear him saying the things he is now saying. I venture even to congratulate him in terms of Holy Writ by saying:
Joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.
The minister will understand the spirit in which I say that.
I wish to read briefly from the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) in the course of this debate, just to show exactly the line he took. This is the line he has taken over the years, not one he has suddenly come to in the last moment, when elections may be in the offlng, and when the need in the eastern provinces has become much more apparent than it was at an earlier time. Speaking on March 6 as reported at page 2704 of Hansard, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, after addressing some remarks to the central provinces about a Canadian pipe line to be built through Canadian territory, said:
In conclusion may I say that I believe it will be a great tragedy if this western gas is not used to supply Canada first.
Having said that he went on to quote Dr. Hume, the oil and gas expert, as follows: The building of an all-Canadian natural gas pipe line from western to eastern Canada could be as important a national asset as was the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway across the preCambrian area.
I draw attention to that phrase "across the pre-Cambrian area", because I suggest that implied in that statement is the fact that when we built across the north shore of Lake Superior it seemed as though every mile was a dead loss. Nevertheless we carried that burden for many years, and we are now beginning to discover that what we thought was a barren waste contained riches the like of which we had never dreamed.
I should like also to quote a sentence from what was said by the then minister of mines in Ontario who, oddly enough, expressed very much the same idea as did Dr. Hume.

Speaking on January 26, 1952, the report in the Globe and Mail states:
Even if it has to be subsidized a pipe line should be built to bring Alberta natural gas to Ontario and Quebec, provincial mines minister Gemmell said here today.
In Ottawa to attend the annual meeting of the Canadian institute of mining and metallurgy, Mr. Gemmell declared that a west-to-east natural gas pipe line was as important to national prosperity today as the C.P.R. was when it was started in the 1870's.
I shall not labour that point further. I just wish to quote another sentence from the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra when, in concluding his observations, he said:
Here is the best chance in our generation to further Canada's development into one of the leading nations of the world: and we must not let that chance slip through our fingers.
I wish to quote from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) who, speaking in the house on March 10 said, as reported at page 2807 of Hansard:
Let us end any uncertainty as to what policy is going to be adopted in a case of this kind. So far as the government are concerned they have left no doubt but that theirs is the ultimate responsibility. Let the government declare that, while it is perfectly true that these are private bills, it is the policy of this government that the first interest to be served will be the interest of the Canadian people.
And continuing the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition:
With regard to these pipe lines, let us have an unqualified declaration of a policy of Canada first in the use of these great resources. That does not mean any dog in the manger attitude in regard to either gas or oil.
And speaking later the same afternoon the Leader of the Opposition made it very clear that he was entirely in favour of the export of gas to the United States, the only condition being that home needs should be satisfied first.
I have read two demands made upon the government by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the Leader of the Opposition. Of course it is not often that the government complies so quickly with requests of that kind, or that it follows so exactly the direction offered to it. How much better the world would be if the government were to do that oftener. I wish now to read what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said on Friday last. If hon. members will recall they will see how meticulously he follows the requests made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the Leader of the Opposition. As reported at page 2929 of Hansard the minister said:
The policy of the government of Canada is to refuse permits for moving natural gas by pipe line
Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited across an international boundary until such time as we are convinced that there can be no economic use, present or future-
I underline the words "present or future", because that covers quite a lot of territory. -until such time as we are convinced that there can be no economic use, present or future, for that natural gas within Canada.
I stress again that that is an exact repetition in ideas, indeed almost a repetition in words, of what had been said by hon. members on this side of the house. I should say that the minister added, a sentence or two later-
The proposal is to follow this policy, within reason.
Well, I would not expect him to apply to it anything else but reason. I stress the fact that it has taken some years to bring the minister to this reasonable attitude, and that he was not always as reasonable as he now appears to be. There was a time when not only was he very unsympathetic but actually was very hostile to the ideas brought forward with great persistence and clarity by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra.
Less than three years ago the minister was pooh-poohing the Canada first suggestion in connection with the Alberta gas application; in fact he was very sharply critical of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. But I suppose two things have happened since that time. First, the arguments respecting the needs of Ontario and Quebec have become much clearer-and I shall have something to say about that later. Second we are approaching the time of an election; and of course anything that can be done to enable the government to claim credit from Ontario and Quebec, as well as from other provinces in Canada, is very important to the government. That could naturally have a great deal to do with declarations of policy. However, as I say, we ought to be very thankful; better late than never.
I have no desire to be ungenerous in welcoming what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said. I do think, however, that I should like to read to the house a letter written by the minister to the premier of Alberta, because I think there are implicit in that letter two or three points I have just made. As I said, the needs of the eastern provinces have become more apparent, and this is referred to in the letter I am about to read. It is a letter of January 2, 1953 from the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the premier of Alberta, and states:
Dear Mr. Manning:
As I am leaving Canada for some five weeks, on a trade mission to South America, I think I should write you about the views of this department regarding the export of natural gas. You are

Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited doubtless aware that this department administers the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act.
We had a conversation about this subject at Sarnia, when Premier Frost was present. At that time, I stated that gas from Alberta must be available to potential customers in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and in the intervening provinces before further export of gas could be authorized.
Well, the minister kept that secret for a very long time, because that was a good many months ago. One would like to know what Premier Frost said to him at that time. It may be that he had some comments to make which crystallized the minister's attitude. Then his letter continues:
This attitude is consistent with the position that the government has taken with regard to the export of hydroelectric power for many years.
Well, that may be the minister's opinion: but it is like pulling teeth for us to get him to indicate any attitude at all. So far as I can recall, last year when many of us on this side of the house were resisting the proposal to have a natural gas pipe line built only as far as Manitoba, the minister was singularly silent. I cannot find that he had anything to say. But now all that is changed. He says:
This attitude is consistent with the position that the government has taken-
Then he goes on to say:
You will appreciate that the supply of gas through a pipe line is analogous with the supply of electric power, in that both demand continuity of supply.
I am aware that, for the period when natural gas is first made available in Ontario and Quebec, and until the load can be built up, such a pipe-line project is unlikely to be profitable, either for the producers of gas or for the owners of the pipeline.
It is most interesting to find the minister taking that line, because we know he used to scold the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) for being bold enough to suggest that there might conceivably be a broad policy in these matters and that possibly the acid test of the last dollar should not finally decide the matter. We now have a broader attitude being taken. The minister went on to say:
Nevertheless there is evidence that a pipe-line project for Ontario and Quebec can be worked out and that the project will be profitable over a period of years.
I am well aware that the government of Canada has no immediate concern with this problem, but I hope that it will be helpful for you to have its views before any definite decisions are taken in Alberta.
That is all I wish to read from the letter. Then later, as reported on the same page 2930 of Hansard, the minister went on to say:
This government has reason to believe that it is economically feasible to build a gas pipe line from southern Alberta to Toronto and Montreal,


serving the intervening Canadian cities, and government policy will require that Canadian gas be used in Canada accordingly.
Then there is a sentence which I read with interest because the minister had said in his letter that the government of Canada had no immediate concern with the problem. This next sentence I suggest rather negatives what he said.
In licensing the export of gas from Alberta, I am sure the government of that province will be disposed to conform with the policy of the federal government in that regard.
I imagine that when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) uses language of that kind people are inclined to think twice before they disagree. I do not believe I need labour the point further. I think it is perfectly clear that the government is now coming forward with this policy. This is a policy which has been advocated on this side for a long time, and therefore we applaud it. We hope no time will be lost in putting it into effect. We hope this measure will not in any way delay the working out of this policy. As I said before, we shall regard ourselves as the parents of this, and the minister only as a lately-arrived step-parent.

Mr. Speaker, the debate on the motion for the second reading of Bill No. 189, to incorporate Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited, has in my judgment covered a most interesting and varied field. It has ranged from the clever and humorous contribution of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), down through the informative speech by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), and finally to the statement of policy made last Friday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. There were other speakers in between, such as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) who made their contributions. If I mention specifically the hon. members for Fraser Valley, Vancouver-Quadra and Port Arthur it is merely to emphasize the breadth of the field that has been covered in this debate, and not merely to single them out as being of particular merit as compared with other speakers.
As I listened to the hon. member for Fraser Valley joust with the mayor of Ottawa I thought what an interesting situation it would be if Charlotte should stand for election to this house, as she has threatened to do, and be successful. I can imagine the day when Ottawa's doughty mayoress takes her place in this house. I will want to have my flash camera here, set at fast speed to get a picture as the hon. member for Fraser Valley marches across the floor gallantly to plant his customary kiss on

Charlotte's dynamic lips. That will be the day and that will be the picture.
I did enjoy the contribution made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley because I think he struggled hard to achieve something that would be worth while, that is to have more speakers take part in this debate, particularly those who might be interested in having for their constituencies a supply of natural gas. I hope the hon. member has succeeded and that there will be more speakers, because I think this debate is well worth while.
The only reason I take part is that I feel I can present a point of view which has not yet been mentioned. If I were merely to repeat what has been said I do not think I would be justified in taking part. My constituency is not on the proposed pipe line and therefore would have nothing to gain from its construction except indirectly. But I do think I have a point of view which hon. members will find interesting. I do not want to be unduly critical when I present it, and I do not mean what I say to be critical in any way.
As the hon. member for Greenwood said, on Friday night the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) placed on record the federal government's policy with respect to natural gas. When I read what the right hon. minister said I decided that in the interests of fairness and of getting at the whole truth I should put on record another statement of policy. The hon. member for Greenwood has quoted the letter written to the premier of Alberta, to be found at page 2930 of Hansard on March 13. I do not intend to repeat that letter, but I do want to repeat a sentence from the minister's remarks which the hon. member for Greenwood quoted and which I think is most interesting. The minister said in referring to the government of Alberta:
I am sure the government of that province will be disposed to conform with the policy of the federal government in that regard.
I should like at this point to put on record a statement of policy which the premier of Alberta made just a week ago in his budget speech delivered in Edmonton. I think hon. members will find it most interesting. I quote from that budget speech by Mr. Manning as follows:
To stimulate continued orderly development of Alberta's vast potential gas reserves, adequate markets for gas surplus to our own requirements are essential, and for this reason it is the policy of the government to approve the export of surplus gas for which no local market is available. As at January 31, 1953, some 300 gas wells representing a capital investment of over $18 million were capped for lack of a market. This situation.
Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited unless corrected, will have a progressively deterring influence on further gas exploration and development and also on the search for oil.
In the Pincher Creek area of southern Alberta, vast supplies of gas, rich in chemical by-products, such as propane, butane and sulphur, remain undeveloped because no adequate market is available in the province for the residue gas remaining after the chemical by-products have been extracted. There is a wide and increasing demand for these by-products within the province and their availability would do much to stimulate further secondary industry.
The government believes the interests of the people of Alberta will be best served by the continued progressive development of their natural resources, both from the standpoint of ensuring for themselves a more abundant supply of products for their own future use and also from the standpoint of sharing in the substantial benefits which will accrue to the province as a whole from such development. It will continue to be the government's policy to protect fully the interests of the people of Alberta by approving for export only gas that has been determined by the petroleum and natural gas conservation board to be surplus to our own requirements, but for the reasons I have outlined it is the government's intention to facilitate the establishment of adequate export markets for such surplus gas at the earliest possible date. In approving the export of surplus gas, the government will adhere to its policy of giving first priority to other Canadian markets if, in the opinion of the board, the economic factors involved are not incompatible with the interests of Alberta producers and the province as a whole.
That is the statement of policy of the Alberta government. I am hoping there will indeed continue to be happy relations between the federal government and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and the government of the province of Alberta and Mr. Manning, who is the minister in charge of development and resources. I sincerely say that; but if that happy relationship is to continue, Mr. Speaker, then the minister is going to have to clarify some of the things he said on Friday night.
I would just like to read two or three excerpts from the minister's statement of last Friday, and the first one I read is from page 2930 of Hansard where, near the bottom of the page, after he had quoted a letter which he had written to Premier Manning on January 2 last, he said:
This letter is of course consistent with the government policy I have outlined. While the government of Alberta has proposals before it which involve the movement of gas eastward and across the United States border to Minneapolis, or through the United States to southern Ontario, permits to that end will not be granted under the terms of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act. This government has reason to believe that it is economically feasible to build a gas line from southern Alberta to Toronto and Montreal serving the intervening Canadian cities and government policy will require that Canadian gas be used in Canada accordingly. In the next column, near the bottom but on the same page, the minister said this:
I am convinced, after thorough study of the matter, that the only reliable supply of natural gas for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec must be from western Canada by means of an allCanadian pipe line.
Mr. Speaker, I am led to ask what that statement means. It would not be surprising to me if the minister's statement had quite considerable political ramifications. Was the Minister of Trade and Commerce talking for Fort William and Port Arthur, or was he talking for all of Canada and the people of Canada? That is a question which I think we have to examine.
I would like to place on record some facts which must be kept in very sharp focus as we proceed to consider any application, I do not care what it is, for a pipe-line charter to carry gas from the province of Alberta to the eastern market. The first consideration is that Albertans sincerely want the development of their oil and gas resources. Second, adequate markets for gas which is surplus to Alberta's needs are essential. If markets! are not obtained then the development cannot go forward, and time is precious. Third, the Alberta government favours and has always favoured a Canada first policy.
Of course, the minister said the other night that it is not "Canada first"; it is "Canada always". Well, I do not mind going along with that, but I think the minister himself has shown a way on various occasions to distinguish between Canada first and Canada always. He himself has done some things and has made some decisions which show that there is a difference. It would not take long to cite them, but that is not my purpose here.
I have placed on the record of this house on several occasions statements by Premier Manning of Alberta to the effect that the Alberta government favours, and always has favoured, a Canada first policy; and if you want to go further and say a Canada always policy, that is all right.
The fourth point is that a pipe line or several pipe lines must be built to carry surplus gas to market. There is no other way by which that gas can reach a market anywhere; only by pipe line.
We are considering now a pipe line to open up possible markets in the provinces east of Alberta. I doubt that it would be possible for a pipe line to pay its costs unless it served a bigger market than is available in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and the cities at the head of the lakes. This means, then, that the Ontario market is essential if the pipe line is to be an economic success or a

financial success. If it is not going to be an economic and financial success it will not be built. We might just as well look at the facts.
Westcoast Transmission Company Limited has already been granted a permit by the Alberta government to carry gas from northern Alberta to the Pacific coast. I understand that the federal Department of Transport has also granted a licence for that exportation of gas. If it has not done so I understand, from the minister's statement, that the government will be prepared to grant the licence. There is some danger, of course, that this line may not materialize because, as many hon. members of this house already know, serious opposition to marketing part of the gas in the United States has already arisen. Interests down there are battling against it and are using their influence with the federal government of the United States to prevent the granting of a licence to bring in that gas. Westcoast Transmission's pipe line would not be economically feasible without the northwestern United States market in addition to the Pacific coast British Columbia market. Development in my constituency, the Alberta Peace river area, and in the British Columbia Peace river area, would not be possible for perhaps many years if Westcoast Transmission's pipe line is not built, that is, if it is found that they cannot get this gas into the northwestern United States.
Those are merely the elementary facts of the situation. I think it would be a very serious blow to northern Alberta and British Columbia, as well as to the Pacific coast and to the whole province, if that pipe line fails to materialize. I am hoping that the good sense of the people in the United States will prevail and they will grant the Westcoast Transmission Company the right to market the surplus at the end of the line in the northwestern United States. I am quite certain, Mr. Speaker, we can guarantee them a continuous supply for many years ahead, and that is one of the important factors in securing and retaining any market. Well, the development of the natural gas resources, and I think perhaps along with them the oil resources, of the Peace river country will probably be delayed many years if the Westcoast Transmission Company or some other pipe-line company fails to build a transmission line from that country to Pacific coast points in British Columbia.
The next point we have to keep in mind is the route to be followed by any pipe line eastward from Alberta. It is a serious concern to many people. There are two main routes which might be taken in an

effort to tap the eastern markets that must be supplied if the huge cost of the line is to be recovered, making the building of it feasible. The first of these is the route directly across the prairie provinces to the head of the lakes, serving Saskatchewan points and Manitoba centres, particularly Winnipeg, and of course Port Arthur and Fort William. The pipe line would then proceed along the northern shore of Lake Superior, perhaps to Sudbury, and then southward into the Toronto area. Such a line might be tapped to supply centres along the way in Ontario as well as in the western provinces. I am sure that my hon. friends, the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) and the member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), appreciate that fact. I do not need to go into the details.
This route would appear to have many advantages that are quite obvious. First, it is an all-Canadian route in keeping with the Canada first or Canada always philosophy, about which so many of the hon. members have shown deep concern. Second, it would supply, besides Saskatchewan centres and Winnipeg, the centres now industrialized such as Fort William and Port Arthur, Sudbury, and then on to the Toronto and western Ontario area. Let me remind hon. members that cheap, clean fuel is a great boon to industrialization. It will do more than anything else to stimulate industrialization. The third advantage of a pipe line along this route would be the possible stimulation of the growth of industries at all the main centres, and perhaps many others, thus contributing to the decentralization or dispersion of industry which is essential to the safety of Canada. Many of us have been talking for a long time about the necessity for the dispersal of industry.
The fourth advantage of the line, as I understand it, is that there might be a substantial income tax write-off on an allCanadian pipe line which may run to as much as $8 million. If that is the case, then I say it is a very substantial consideration from the financial point of view in building this great line. I think perhaps there would not be the same advantage if the line were built partly through the United States. There are possibly many other obvious advantages to this route which I cannot take the time now to list. But there are some very serious disadvantages to this route which must be recognized and taken into consideration. I should like to set them out as well.

Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited First, the distance to be spanned to reach the one market that must be served, if the project is able to pay, is very great. The minister pointed that out in the first part of his statement the other day when he was dealing with the arguments relative to the transportation of petroleum. He showed that there was a difference of something like 400 miles in the length of the route into the Sarnia area. The line that we have been discussing around the northern shores of the lakes would be traversing between 800 and
1,000	miles of wilderness.
The second disadvantage is that rock formation extends for most of that 1,000 miles of wilderness. Everyone knows that it is very costly to build pipe lines through heavy rock formation. Third, the cost of maintenance would be high because there is no road along the route, and to build roads through that area would be a rather costly business. We are finding that out already in attempting to build this trans-Canada highway.
I think I can safely say that the economics of this route have not, as yet, been proven sufficiently to make an all-Canadian pipe line feasible, although the minister said the other day that his studies have convinced him that it was feasible economically. I say that I doubt that very much. However, the ultimate economics of an all-Canadian route may be proven to be better than those of a route farther south. If so, then we most certainly favour that all-Canadian route, and let me make that abundantly clear.
At this stage, however, it seems to me to be silly to lay down the requirement that this Mid-Continent pipe line follow an allCanadian route until we know, and until we are sure, that the economics are sound. Now, with all of the disadvantages of the route which I have listed, I think it may be foolish to require that this route should be the only one we consider. Any statement by anyone in this house, minister or other member, that lays down the requirement that this is the only route we will consider-Mr. Speaker, that is not good thinking.
The second possible route is one following roughly the Interprovincial pipe line right of way to Superior, Wisconsin, thence through the area south of Lake Superior in the United States to the straits of Mackinac, and from there by way of Port Huron and Sarnia into the Toronto and southwestern Ontario market. In time, of course, an extension of this line might be made even as far as Montreal. This would not be an allCanadian route, but it could be made to serve an all-Canadian market, which simply means that provisions of the licence and

Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited permit might be such as to prohibit the sale of any of the gas carried by the line in the United States. If such in-bond provisions, as the minister called them the other night, are feasible-and I think they are-then this route too could be said to come within the Canada first or Canada always policy. I should like to emphasize that. It could very easily come completely within that Canada first or Canada always policy that has been discussed.
There is considerable evidence that the economics of a pipe line along the southern route would be better than the economics of the all-Canadian route, although I believe not enough facts are yet available to most of us on which to base a final judgment. Two facts do stand out, however, which seem to favour this southern route. The first of these is that the distance to the essential market in Ontario is much shorter, perhaps as much as 350 miles. Hence the cost would be very substantially less. When you start to build a 30-inch pipe line, 350 miles of it runs into a lot of money. This fact was stressed by the minister the other day. The second obvious advantage would be that soil conditions and terrain along the route are considerably less costly to build through. On all of these counts, the route would be cheaper in the end.
I have stressed the economics of the routes in what I have said today, Mr. Speaker, and you may ask why. While it is urgent and essential that markets be found for gas which is surplus to Alberta's needs; while we are anxious for development of resources in that province; and also while we want Canadian markets to have priority over foreign markets, we must not let political or emotional considerations force Alberta gas producers to subsidize either the eastern market or the pipe line that carries the gas from Alberta to that market. I want to make that point abundantly clear.
What do I mean by that? Mr. Speaker,
I mean simply that the field price to Alberta producers must be fair and such as to ensure, first, that they can stay in business in a state of good economic health and, second, that sufficient inducement will be provided for continued exploration and development of that great resource.
The eastern market, as everybody knows, can pay only so much for gas delivered to it. The pipe line will have to charge so much to carry the gas across a vast distance to the market. If the laid-down price to eastern consumers is too high, they will not buy it. On the other hand, they will try to force either the pipe-line company or the producers of the gas to reduce their 

prices. The Alberta government is determined that, under any permits which they grant for the export of gas from that province, the field price to producers must be fair and just, and must remain fair and just. For that reason, and also because we should like to see prairie province and eastern Canadian consumers able to procure their gas supply at reasonable cost, we maintain that the economics of the various possible routes must be most carefully considered and that route be chosen which will achieve the purposes which I have stated. Otherwise we are doing an immeasurable injustice to everybody concerned, and we are not taking action that is in the best interests of Canada as a whole.
Under the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, with all these things in mind, may I say this. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said as reported at page 2930 of Hansard:
While the government of Alberta has proposals before it which involve the movement of gas eastward and across the United States border to Minneapolis, or through the United States to southern Ontario, permits to that end will not be granted under the terms of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act.
I think the minister was being just a little bit silly in his statement the other night.

Mr. Speaker, I think hon. members will agree, after listening to the discussion today, that it is high time the committee got together to discuss the problem of broadcasting in Canada. Broadcasting and telecasting, as we know today, deal with a means of communication that is very important. It seems to me, as I have listened to the discussion, that there is an unfortunate lack of communication of ideas in this chamber. It is either a semantics problem, misrepresentation of the meaning of meanings, or it is a deliberate attempt to obscure the issue.
On several occasions today we have been discussing the problem as if it is a case of C.B.C. or no C.B.C.; control or no control. Since I came into this house I have had the privilege of sitting in one series of committee meetings on broadcasting, and I have not gathered the impression that it was a case of that kind. No one is presenting the proposition that Canada would be much better off without the C.B.C. We all recognize the excellent job it has done in the establishment of a suitable broadcasting medium in this country. Particularly no one on this side can be accused of that viewpoint, because it was the policy of this party that first initiated the present organization and started it on its successful career in Canada.
I say too that it is not a matter of control or no control, as some have attempted to present it in this chamber today. We all acknowledge that there must be some form of control over a communication medium as important and significant as is the broadcasting and telecasting field. I do not think we are getting very far when we discuss this problem in an emotional tone as it has been discussed today.
I suppose I should regard myself as a junior member. That is a category that was given expression to by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) the other day; although I did think, until I came into the chamber and became aware of the atmosphere of discrimination, that regardless of seniority, as far as the number of years or length of time was concerned, we were all equal before the Speaker of the house. As that category or designation has been used, as a junior member perhaps I should not be too critical; but I will go this far and say that there have been some strong emotional expressions in this chamber which do not reflect very creditably upon the statesmanlike deliberations of the house.

Special Committee on Broadcasting
I do not think this will be unparliamentary, but I would like to say that some of the techniques that have been used in the house today are like the Russian techniques. They tell me that as you enter East Berlin from West Berlin, although I have not had that privilege, there is a sign just at the border: "You are now entering the democratic part of Germany". From our viewpoint, of course, we believe that just the reverse is the case, that as soon as you cross from west to east you are entering the totalitarian section. However, our totalitarian friends, the Russians, are very clever in the use of both the small lie and the big lie to put their opponents on the defensive. We know what they have done with the meaning of such words as "democracy" and "peace". They have completely obscured the issues by drawing red herrings across the trail and by distorting the traditional meanings of words.
We have heard today accusations thrown across the chamber that the Conservative party is against the C.B.C. I think it is an attempt to obscure the issue and place this group on the defensive, so that it has to begin from a position of disadvantage. In the first instance, we do not have to apologize to anyone, because it was during the Conservative administration that the present broadcasting policy was established. I have been interested to hear members or groups, including the C.C.F. group, giving due credit to the late Mr. Bennett in this regard. It is just unfortunate that they would not give him as much credit for his other efforts as they do for this particular policy.
While recognizing that broadcasting is a very important medium of communication, and while recognizing that communication is basic to the successful continuation of our democratic way of life, I do not subscribe to the viewpoint which seems to be expressed from a number of sources that broadcasting and telecasting are the beginning and end of the solution of communication difficulties. The late Dr. Harold Innis, who has dealt extensively with the problem of communication in relation to civilization and can be regarded as an authority in the field, summed up a lifetime of thinking on the subject in his book called "Communication and Empire." He pointed out that each succeeding civilization which had achieved notable progress and development, the Babylonian, Egyptian, Grecian and Roman, had its success largely conditioned and determined by the medium of communication used most frequently. The Babylonians were limited by the use of the stylus and the clay tablet; the Egyptians by the quill and papyrus; the Romans were restricted by almost the same medium. So far as the flourishing Greek civilization was
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
concerned he points out that they developed the oral medium to a new high level, so that the golden age of Greece was largely a reflection of their successful adoption of a more flexible oral tradition.
He goes on in the development of his theme to deal with modem media, particularly mass media of communication. He points out that, rather than stimulating civilization or encouraging true creative cultural development, it would possibly have the effect of discouraging that development because in dealing with the cinema, radio and television we are dealing with a mechanized media. Instead of creativity, you have rigidity. You have robots produced rather than responsible creative individuals. I am inclined to agree that there is a lot of truth in what he says.
When we approach this problem, therefore, from the standpoint that television and broadcasting are going to solve all the problems that we find existing in Canadian cultural development, I think we are taking a theme that has no essence in reality. Actually, we do not solve any of our problems unless we deal with the basic institutions that are responsible for forming citizens' in a democratic society, for developing their ideas, for developing their conscience and their outlook on life. Those basic institutions are the home, the school and the church. If they are doing their job, none of these hair-raising murder stories, none of these so-called dangerous influences that have been criticized here tonight, can make their impact on the developing mind of the individual because the pattern of the personality is established in the matrix of these other more important institutions.
Perhaps we are dealing with a straw man. It is repeatedly put forward in magazine articles, and you can read it in many speeches, that we are dealing with the most important media of communication that has ever confronted man. It is said that the way we use it is going to determine our future destiny. This sounds impressive, and it sounds convincing, but it cannot be substantiated if you examine the thesis critically.
I turn now to the Massey report on the arts, letters and sciences, that very famous document which is often used to support this viewpoint. The Massey commission has made a great contribution to Canada by pointing out the problem of cultural development in this country. We were aware of it in a vague way; but by bringing together in one volume all the thinking of the various leaders in this field they have brought the problem into focus. Actually the briefs presented to the Massey commission came largely from

professional sources, those who had a professional interest in culture. It may be that their emphasis on the difficulty does not get down to the grass roots difficulty. I do believe that in dealing with the contribution that broadcasting and telecasting can make toward the solution of the relatively slow progress of the development of a distinct Canadian culture, the commission missed one fundamental point. I have already mentioned this point, but I repeat that mass media are not necessarily the solution to this difficulty.
As I have pointed out, mass media are impersonal. They make mass impressions on a non-responsive audience, an audience that is sitting inert and not necessarily reacting to the impressions that are made upon their minds. It is as the late Dr. Innis described, a mechanization of knowledge which is more likely to turn out a generation of robots than a generation of intellectual and cultural giants. It is a basic truism that in order for communication to be effective in shaping the thinking of a people or shaping the personality of a people, there must be interaction. You cannot sit unresponsively and absorb impressions. You must react. There must be a mutual reaction and impression, and this is the one big deficiency both in the fields of broadcasting and telecasting. If radio and television in Canada are going to make an even larger contribution to this important field than they have in the past, we must develop machinery for inter-action to a more efficient level than we have up to this time.
For example, one of the attempts of the C.B.C. to keep in touch with the public is through the C.B.C. Radio Times, a little publication that is circulated monthly. I believe the subscription fee is $1, and I understand the total circulation of that magazine is something like 12,000 copies, not a very large circulation. It might be necessary also to have some sort of advisory council which is constantly in touch with the reactions of the public to the programs being presented by the C.B.C., and in turn indicating these impressions to the board of governors so that a closer contact might be realized. That policy, I might say, is already in effect with regard to British Broadcasting Corporation activities.
Moving on in this discussion, today we have had several specific difficulties presented with regard to broadcasting in Canada. It has been pointed out that one of the purposes of the establishment of the C.B.C. was to assure that broadcasting would have a distinct Canadian flavour. Of course, when we say that we are thinking of the possible impact of the more populous and powerful United States nation to the south 68108-1941
Special Committee on Broadcasting of us. I might suggest one or two criticisms in this regard. They will be coming up for consideration, when the committee meets. One of the programs that is most obnoxious from my standpoint and that comes over the C.B.C. are these perpetual emotional binges, the soap operas, that grind relentlessly on day after day. I note that it is the C.B.C., not the private broadcasters, which is the chief offender in this regard. Apparently the revenue source in advertising is substantial and has been necessary to maintain the C.B.C. programs.
So far as the idea of putting up a screen against United States influence is concerned, I think it is going to be even more difficult in the television age mainly because Americans have a head start in the field; they have developed techniques that are in advance of ours and they have a large number of people skilled in the use of the television medium. Hence they are inevitably going to make their impact upon us.
I have not seen much television. Recently when I was in the city of Toronto I had my first opportunity to see C.B.C. television. 1 was interested to note that already United States programs are being used over the C.B.C. television station-I think it is CBTL -in Toronto. Actually we are again dealing with a straw man with regard to this business of promoting Canadianism by broadcasting only. It is much like the panacea viewpoint that is held with regard to all broadcasting and telecasting activities. Canadianism is not going to be established by mass media of communication. Inevitably we are going to be subjected to outside and so-called foreign influences in this modern age of communication and speed of transportation, which brings us closely together as neighbours not only with the United States but with every part of the world.
If I may, I am going to quote from an expert in the field of culture who does a little bit of leg pulling on this score. Actually we all tend to be ethnocentric. We tend to view the world from our own standards and to believe that everybody is crazy but ourselves. We are a little bit ethnocentric in this emphasis on Canadianism in the mass media. The gentleman I quote is speaking from a United States viewpoint but we might well apply what he says to the Canadian viewpoint as well. He is a man called Ralph Linton and writing in the American Mercury he says:
There can be no question about the average American's Americanism or his desire to preserve this precious heritage at all costs. Nevertheless, some insidious foreign ideas have already wormed their way into his civilization without his realizing what was going on.

Special Committee on Broadcasting
He now proceeds to go through a typical day in the average American's life.
Thus dawn finds the unsuspecting patriot garbed in pajamas, a garment of East Indian origin; and lying in a bed built on a pattern which originated in either Persia or Asia Minor. He is muffled to the ears in un-American materials; cotton, first domesticated in India; linen, domesticated in the Near East; wool from an animal native to Asia Minor; or silk whose uses were first discovered by the Chinese. All these substances have been transformed into cloth by methods invented in southwestern Asia. If the weather is cold enough he may even be sleeping under an eiderdown quilt invented in Scandinavia.
On awakening he glances at the clock, a medieval European invention, uses one potent Latin word in abbreviated form, rises in haste, and goes to the bathroom. Here, if he stops to think about it, he must feel himself in the presence of a great American institution; he will have heard stories of both the quality and frequency of foreign plumbing and will know that in no other country does the average man perform his ablutions in the midst of such splendor. But the insidious foreign influence pursues him even here.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Will the hon. gentleman tell me what this fairy tale has to do with the setting up of a committee on the C.B.C.?
It resembles the government's policy on television.
